idea: The 1499 Lyon 'La grant danse macabre' woodcut, the earliest known picture of a printing shop, where skeletons grab the compositor and pressman, with one word underneath: 'Deadline.' A 500-year-old print-shop joke for anyone who has ever been chased by a due date.

An 18th-century engraving of a compositor's two type cases, capitals in the upper case and small letters in the lower, captioned 'Lowercase was a place.' Typography nerds get the real origin of the word, and everyone else learns something.

An engraving of a stereotype foundry casting a plate from set type, captioned 'Stereotype and cliché were both printing plates. Cast once, repeated forever.' It's a true etymology that doubles as a quiet argument against lazy thinking.
The 1631 'Wicked Bible' page with its missing 'not', so it reads 'Thou shalt commit adultery.', and a small caption: 'Proofread. (Barker & Lucas, fined £300.)' The best shirt ever made for an editor.

Jean Le Tavernier's c. 1456 portrait of the scribe Jean Miélot at his desk, quill in one hand and penknife in the other, captioned 'The knife was the delete key.' Medieval scribes really did scrape mistakes off vellum, and the shirt makes that ordinary detail land.

An engraved monk bent over his manuscript with a real scribal colophon formula: 'Explicit hoc totum. Pro Christo da mihi potum.' Under it, small: 'That's the whole thing. For Christ's sake, give me a drink.' It's funny and true, and it gets you a drink at the pub.

Aldus Manutius's dolphin-and-anchor printer's mark, first used in Venice in 1502, with its motto translated: 'Make haste slowly.' Five centuries of good advice from the man who brought out pocket-sized books and italic type.

An early printed page with the empty space at a paragraph opening circled, captioned 'The indent is where the pilcrow used to be.' It points to the story that printers left gaps for rubricators to hand-paint ¶ marks, and sometimes nobody came back to fill them.

A huge, ornate 18th-century Caslon italic ampersand captioned 'and per se and'. The word ampersand comes from schoolchildren reciting '& per se and' at the end of the alphabet. A beautiful letterform that comes with a real story.

Josse Bade's 'Prelum Ascensianum' device, an early woodcut of a wooden hand press, captioned 'Press (n.): the machine, then the people, then the pressure they apply.' One word's history, from the press to journalism to accountability.

An archive engraving of an ox's head that turns, step by step, into a capital A, captioned 'A is an ox, upside down.' The letter does come from the Phoenician aleph, an ox, and the drawing shows the whole history of the alphabet in one line.

A 19th-century engraving of the Rosetta Stone captioned 'Same decree. Three scripts. The Greek let the dead talk again.' The stone carries one text in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, and that is how Champollion cracked hieroglyphs in 1822. A shirt about translation as resurrection.

An engraving of a chained medieval book on a library lectern, like the ones still at Hereford Cathedral, with two words: 'Reference only.' Dry library humor that also says how precious books once were.

Reynolds' portrait of Samuel Johnson, engraved, with his real 1755 Dictionary entry: 'Lexicographer: A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.' Self-deprecation from the man who defined the language, for anyone who loves words a bit too much.

An engraving of Hammersmith Bridge with tiny metal sorts falling into the water, captioned 'Doves Type. Thrown into the Thames, 1916–17, so nobody else could have it.' Cobden-Sanderson really did drown his typeface, and divers recovered some of it in 2014. Typographic devotion taken to an extreme.

The 1878 patent drawing of the Sholes and Glidden QWERTY keyboard, captioned 'Designed for a typewriter in the 1870s. You're still using it.' Your daily keyboard is a 19th-century fossil, and the shirt shows how long a design decision can last.

The Droeshout engraving of Shakespeare from the 1623 First Folio, captioned 'Saved by printers. 18 of his plays survive only because two friends published them.' A tribute to Heminges and Condell, and a reminder that literature lives or dies by publishing.

A drawing of the real 1445 Dubrovnik manuscript page with a cat's inky paw prints walked across the text, captioned 'Peer review, 1445.' The joke is cute, but the point underneath is serious: archives keep the accidents too.

Carl Spitzweg's 'The Bookworm' (1850), the old scholar on a library ladder with books under his arm and between his knees, in one-colour line, captioned 'Came for one book.' Every reader who has ever lost an afternoon in the stacks knows the feeling.

A big engraved 16th-century manicule, the pointing hand readers drew in margins, pointing up at the wearer's face, with a small caption: 'manicule (n.): the reader's hand. Pointing at what matters since the Middle Ages.' A good-looking piece of reading history that turns the wearer into the bit worth noticing.
